terms.plain: A profit split calculated one deal at a time, so the manager can earn its share on early winners before the rest of the fund is resolved. Faster for the manager, and the reason clawbacks exist.
terms.formal: A deal-by-deal distribution structure permitting carried interest on individual realisations before whole-fund capital return, typically paired with escrow accounts and clawback protection.

terms.plain: A demand from a fund for investors to send in some of the money they committed. Private funds draw capital down as deals happen rather than taking it all up front.
terms.formal: A notice requiring limited partners to transfer a portion of their committed capital, typically to fund an investment or expenses, within a short specified period.

terms.plain: The manager's share of the profits, usually around 20%, paid only above a minimum return. It is the main way private fund managers get paid.
terms.formal: The general partner's share of fund profits, typically 20% above a preferred return, distributed according to the fund's waterfall provisions.

terms.plain: A stretch of the profit split where the manager takes most or all of the cash, to catch up to its full profit share after investors have received their preferred return.
terms.formal: A waterfall tier in which the general partner receives an accelerated share of distributions, often 50% to 100%, until it has received its full carried interest percentage of cumulative profits.

terms.plain: A promise by the manager to hand back profit share it was paid earlier, if later losses mean it ended up taking more than its agreed share of the fund's lifetime profits.
terms.formal: A contractual obligation requiring the general partner to return previously distributed carried interest so that lifetime distributions conform to the agreed profit split.

terms.plain: A chance to put extra money directly into one specific deal alongside the fund, usually at lower or no fees. Highly prized, and usually offered to the largest investors first.
terms.formal: A direct investment in a portfolio company made alongside a fund by one of its limited partners, typically on reduced or zero fee and carried interest terms.

terms.plain: The total amount you promise to a private fund. Only part of it is called at any time, so the money must stay available for years.
terms.formal: The aggregate capital an investor contractually agrees to provide to a fund over its investment period, drawn down through capital calls rather than funded at closing.

terms.plain: The moment a performance fee stops being a paper accrual and is actually taken by the manager, usually at year end. Once taken it is not returned if the fund later falls.
terms.formal: The periodic conversion of accrued performance fees into realised fees payable to the manager, resetting the reference level from which future fees are calculated.

terms.plain: Cash actually returned divided by cash actually called. The one private markets figure that cannot be argued with, because it is realised money.
terms.formal: Cumulative distributions divided by paid-in capital, measuring realised return without reliance on unrealised valuations.

terms.plain: Committed capital a fund has not yet called or invested. High industry dry powder means more competition for deals and usually higher entry prices.
terms.formal: Undrawn committed capital available for investment, whose aggregate level across a strategy is an indicator of competitive pressure on entry valuations.

terms.plain: A profit split calculated across the whole fund, so the manager earns its share only once every investor's capital and preferred return have been paid back. Slower for the manager, safer for investors.
terms.formal: A whole-of-fund distribution structure in which carried interest arises only after aggregate contributed capital and preferred return have been returned to limited partners.

terms.plain: An arrangement where fees the manager collects from the companies it owns are credited back against the management fee you pay. The share credited is negotiable, and worth checking.
terms.formal: A provision crediting a specified proportion of transaction, monitoring and other portfolio company fees received by the general partner against limited partners' management fee obligations.

terms.plain: A limit on how much can be redeemed from a fund in one period. It protects remaining investors from a rush for the exit, and traps you if you wanted out.
terms.formal: A provision capping aggregate or per-investor redemptions in a given period, designed to prevent forced liquidation of illiquid assets at the expense of remaining holders.

terms.plain: The firm that runs the fund: it finds the deals, makes the decisions and gets paid a fee plus a share of the profits. Usually the manager sitting across the table from you.
terms.formal: The partner holding management authority and unlimited liability in a limited partnership, responsible for investment decisions and fund operations, compensated through management fees and carried interest.

terms.plain: The highest value your account has ever reached. A hedge fund can charge performance fees only on gains above it, so losses have to be earned back before fees resume.
terms.formal: The peak net asset value per unit on which performance fees have previously been charged; subsequent fees accrue only on appreciation above that level.

terms.plain: The return the fund must beat before the manager earns any share of the profits. Often 8% a year in private funds.
terms.formal: The minimum return threshold that must be achieved before the general partner participates in fund profits.

terms.plain: The shape a private fund's returns trace over its life: negative early on, because fees are charged and investments have not matured, then rising as investments are sold. Plotted over time it looks like the letter J.
terms.formal: The characteristic trajectory of a closed-end private fund's cumulative net return, initially negative due to fees and unrealised early-stage holdings, then improving as value is realised.

terms.plain: An investor in the fund. Puts up the money, has no say in individual deals, and cannot lose more than it committed.
terms.formal: A passive investor in a limited partnership whose liability is capped at its committed capital and who does not participate in day-to-day investment decisions.

terms.plain: The contract setting out every rule of the fund: the fees, how profits are split, how long it lasts, what the manager may and may not do. Everything you are told verbally should be in here.
terms.formal: The governing document of a limited partnership, specifying economic terms, investment restrictions, governance rights, reporting obligations, term and dissolution mechanics.

terms.plain: A period during which you cannot get your money out of a fund at all.
terms.formal: A contractual period following investment during which redemption is prohibited, used to match investor liquidity to the underlying strategy's horizon.

terms.plain: An annual fee charged simply for managing the money, typically 1.5% to 2%. Paid whether the fund makes money or not, which is why the base it is charged on matters so much.
terms.formal: A recurring fee charged on committed capital, invested capital or net asset value depending on the stage of the fund's life, intended to cover the manager's operating costs.

terms.plain: Total value divided by money invested. A 2.5x MOIC means you got two and a half times your money back — but it says nothing about how long that took.
terms.formal: The ratio of total realised and unrealised value to invested capital, insensitive to timing and therefore quoted alongside IRR.

terms.plain: A clause letting an investor see the side deals other investors were given and elect the same terms. Usually restricted to investors who committed at least as much as they did.
terms.formal: A provision entitling a limited partner to review side letter terms granted to other investors and to elect to adopt them, commonly subject to commitment-size tiers.

terms.plain: What a fund is worth: everything it owns minus everything it owes. Exposures are quoted as a percentage of it, so 130% long means long positions worth 1.3 times the fund's capital.
terms.formal: Total fund assets less total liabilities, the denominator against which exposures, leverage and per-unit values are expressed.

terms.plain: The first slice of profit, which goes entirely to investors before the manager takes anything. Usually 8% a year on the money actually drawn down.
terms.formal: A priority return to limited partners, typically 8% compounded annually on contributed capital, distributed in full before the general partner receives carried interest.

terms.plain: How much warning you must give a hedge fund before pulling money out: 30, 60 or 90 days is typical. Combined with how often the fund lets people out, it determines how fast you can actually get cash.
terms.formal: The contractually required advance notification period an investor must provide before a redemption is effected on a permitted dealing date.

terms.plain: What the fund still holds, at the manager's own valuation, divided by cash called. It is an estimate, not a result.
terms.formal: Unrealised net asset value divided by paid-in capital, representing the portion of reported performance dependent on the manager's valuations.

terms.plain: Buying an existing investor's stake in a private fund, or a portfolio of assets, from them rather than committing to a new fund. Usually at a discount.
terms.formal: Transactions in existing private fund interests or asset portfolios, providing liquidity to sellers and typically transacted at a discount to reported net asset value.

terms.plain: A private agreement giving one investor terms the others do not have: lower fees, better reporting, more information rights. It is legally part of that investor's deal, not the fund's main contract.
terms.formal: A bilateral agreement between the general partner and an individual limited partner that modifies or supplements the partnership agreement as it applies to that investor.

terms.plain: A part of a fund holding assets that cannot be valued or sold normally, carved out so the rest of the fund can still be redeemed.
terms.formal: A segregated portion of a fund containing illiquid or hard-to-value positions, excluded from ordinary redemption and realised separately.

terms.plain: A credit facility a fund uses to pay for deals before calling investor money. It shortens the period investor capital is outstanding, which raises the reported IRR.
terms.formal: A revolving credit facility secured against limited partner commitments, used to defer capital calls and thereby compress the measurement period over which IRR is calculated.

terms.plain: Everything the fund is worth — cash returned plus what it still holds — divided by cash called. Early in a fund's life it is mostly the manager's own opinion.
terms.formal: The sum of distributions and residual value divided by paid-in capital. Equals DPI plus RVPI, and is dominated by unrealised marks in a fund's early years.

terms.plain: The year a private fund started investing. It largely determines the prices it paid and the conditions it exited into, which is why funds are compared within vintages.
terms.formal: The year in which a fund makes its first investment, used as the primary basis for peer comparison because entry pricing, credit availability and exit conditions are cycle-dependent.

terms.plain: The order in which cash coming out of a fund gets paid out: who receives what, and in what sequence. Each tier fills completely before the next receives anything.
terms.formal: The contractual sequence governing distribution of fund proceeds across return of capital, preferred return, catch-up and residual profit split tiers.
